name: Delgocitinib
lead: Delgocitinib is a topical Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor used on the skin of the hands and body to calm eczema. By reducing the redness, scaling, cracking and itch of inflamed skin, it helps people get smoother, calmer-looking skin, and hands in particular are among the most visible parts of a person's presentation. It is sold as Anzupgo (cream) in the United States and Europe and as an ointment in Japan.[1][2]

The US label covers moderate to severe chronic hand eczema in adults who have had an inadequate response to topical corticosteroids or for whom steroids are not advisable. The drug inhibits JAK1, JAK2, JAK3 and tyrosine kinase 2 (TYK2), which blocks signalling by several inflammatory cytokines in the skin.[1] Japan approved a delgocitinib ointment for atopic dermatitis in adults and children in 2020.[2][3]

Two phase 3 trials (DELTA 1 and DELTA 2) compared a 2% cream with vehicle for 16 weeks in adults with chronic hand eczema, and a later head-to-head trial compared it with oral alitretinoin.[4][5] Researchers have also begun small trials of the cream in scarring hair-loss conditions such as frontal fibrosing alopecia.[6][7]

chain: Blocks JAK-driven inflammatory signalling in the skin
Less redness, scaling, fissuring and itch
angle.text: Delgocitinib is a prescription anti-inflammatory applied to eczema-affected skin. As flares settle, the visible redness, flaking and cracking of the hands recede, which is how it improves appearance. It is prescribed for chronic hand eczema rather than for general cosmetic use.

paras: The US-labelled use is the topical treatment of moderate to severe chronic hand eczema in adults whose disease has not responded adequately to topical corticosteroids or who cannot use them. The label advises against combining it with other JAK inhibitors or potent immunosuppressants.[1]

In Japan the ointment is approved for atopic dermatitis in adults and children.[2][3] Reviews of topical atopic dermatitis therapy list delgocitinib alongside ruxolitinib cream and tapinarof as newer non-steroid options.[8]

In the DELTA 1 and DELTA 2 phase 3 trials, adults with moderate to severe chronic hand eczema applied 2% delgocitinib cream or vehicle twice daily for 16 weeks. Treatment success (clear or almost clear on the investigator's global assessment) was reached by 20% versus 10% of participants in DELTA 1 and 29% versus 7% in DELTA 2. Adverse event rates were similar between groups.[4]

A 52-week open-label extension (DELTA 3) reported long-term safety and efficacy, and a quality-of-life analysis of the phase 3 programme has also been published.[9][10] A 16-week phase 2b trial had earlier shown a dose response.[11]

In DELTA FORCE, 513 adults with severe chronic hand eczema were randomised to delgocitinib cream or oral alitretinoin. Hand eczema severity scores fell more with the cream at week 12, and fewer people on the cream reported adverse events (49% versus 76%), with headache much less frequent.[5]

Japanese phase 3 studies of the ointment in adults and children with atopic dermatitis have also been published.[12][13] A phase 2 trial of the cream in frontal fibrosing alopecia examined changes in the molecular signature of lesions, and further trials in hair-loss conditions are registered.[6][14]

The US label lists application-site pain, paresthesia, itching, redness and bacterial skin infections such as paronychia and cellulitis among reactions seen in up to 1% of trial participants. Warnings cover serious infections (one case of eczema herpeticum was seen) and non-melanoma skin cancers, and periodic skin examinations are advised.[1]
Data on use in pregnancy are insufficient to assess risk; animal studies at high oral doses showed no developmental effects.[1]

Delgocitinib inhibits JAK1, JAK2, JAK3 and TYK2, interrupting signalling through STAT proteins that drives cytokine-responsive gene expression. The label notes that the precise mechanism in chronic hand eczema is not known.[1]

Japan was the first to approve delgocitinib, as an ointment for atopic dermatitis in 2020.[2][3] LEO Pharma later developed a cream for chronic hand eczema, studied in the DELTA programme and sold as Anzupgo.[4][1]

timeline.event: Delgocitinib ointment approved in Japan for atopic dermatitis.[2]
DELTA 1 and DELTA 2 phase 3 results published in The Lancet.[4]
DELTA FORCE head-to-head trial against alitretinoin published; Anzupgo cream carries a US label for chronic hand eczema.[5][1]

card.summary: A prescription topical JAK-inhibitor cream that calms chronic hand eczema, leaving hands smoother and less red and cracked.
card.note: Prescription only; label warns of infections and non-melanoma skin cancers.

quick.overview:
Delgocitinib is a steroid-free prescription cream that treats chronic hand eczema. Calming the inflammation reduces the redness, scaling, cracking and itch that make hands look and feel rough.

In two phase 3 trials, more adults reached clear or almost clear hands on the cream than on vehicle after 16 weeks, and a head-to-head trial found larger severity improvements than oral alitretinoin.
quick.mechanism: It blocks JAK1, JAK2, JAK3 and TYK2, enzymes that relay inflammatory cytokine signals inside skin cells, so the immune-driven inflammation in eczema quietens.
quick.risks: Labelled adverse reactions are uncommon and include application-site pain, itching, and skin infections; the label warns about serious infections and non-melanoma skin cancer. It is prescription only, and pregnancy data are insufficient.
